➡️ South Korea confirms 22% crypto tax will cover private wallets, foreign exchanges 

🌐 South Korea has confirmed that taxable crypto income earned through overseas exchanges and private wallets will fall under its planned 22% digital asset tax when the regime takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027. Digital Asset reported on Aug. 20, citing government responses submitted to People Power Party lawmaker Kim Sang-hoon, that the Ministry of Economy and Finance and the National Tax Service said the location or custody method of a digital asset would not determine whether income from its transfer or lending is taxable. 

⭐️ Under the current framework, income from digital assets will be classified as other income, with an annual basic deduction of 2.5 million won. Income exceeding that threshold will face a 20% national tax, rising to a maximum combined rate of 22% after local income tax. The government also maintained that the tax should take effect on schedule next year, even as the People Power Party continues to call for its abolition or another delay.

⚡️ The National Tax Service said income earned by South Korean residents through the transfer or lending of digital assets would remain taxable regardless of whether the assets were held on an overseas exchange or in a private wallet. The Finance Ministry gave a similar response, saying the tax treatment does not depend on whether the income originated domestically or overseas. Transactions made through private wallets will also be treated under the same principle.

American Jews themselves are politically diverse. Many are liberal Democrats and have been deeply critical of Trump. Others are conservative Republicans and some became enthusiastic supporters of his Israel policies. 

Orthodox Jewish communities, evangelical Christians, pro-Israel organizations, wealthy donors, Republican strategists and Israeli officials all interacted with the Trump administration in different ways.

That diversity is precisely why the story is more interesting than a simple claim about “Jewish influence.” What we see instead is a series of relationships.

A Jewish New York lawyer, Roy Cohn, helped teach a young Trump how to fight and how to use publicity as a weapon.

A television industry turned that New York persona into a national brand.

Trump's daughter entered an Orthodox Jewish family through her marriage to Jared Kushner, bringing one of America's most prominent Jewish real-estate families into the president's immediate family circle. Kushner became a senior political adviser.

Friedman and Greenblatt brought their own views, networks and experience into Trump's foreign-policy operation.

And the resulting administration made decisions on Jerusalem, the Golan Heights, Iran and Arab-Israeli normalization that fundamentally changed American Middle East policy.

There is another dimension to this story as well: Trump's own understanding of Jewish success.

Throughout his career, Trump repeatedly operated in environments where he encountered successful Jewish businessmen, lawyers, media executives and political figures. Sometimes his comments about Jews were crude or stereotypical; sometimes they were admiring; often they reflected the transactional worldview through which he understood almost every relationship.

Trump tends to see politics through people rather than institutions — who is loyal, who is useful, who has access, who can negotiate, who can deliver. In that sense, the individuals around him mattered enormously. Personal relationships often became channels through which policy was shaped.

And that may be the most important point. The history of Trump's relationship with Jewish America is not the history of a president being controlled by “the Jews.” There is no evidence for such a collective explanation, and it reduces a complicated political history to an ethnic stereotype.

The real story is more concrete — and arguably more fascinating.

For decades, Trump moved through a particular New York ecosystem of lawyers, developers, financiers, entertainers and media figures. Some of the people who became important to him were Jewish. Some were not. What mattered was not their ethnicity alone, but their individual influence, access, expertise and ability to operate inside the worlds Trump trusted.

By the time he reached the White House, many of those relationships had evolved into a political network.

The journey from Roy Cohn's Manhattan office to the Oval Office, from The Apprentice to Jerusalem, was not a straight line. But it reveals something fundamental about Trump: his politics did not emerge from nowhere in 2016. They were built over decades, in the institutions and relationships of New York — and some of the most consequential figures along that path were Jewish.

Trump's relationship with Jewish America and Israel, in other words, did not begin in the White House.

It began much earlier — in the boardrooms, courtrooms, television studios and social networks of New York.

And by the time Trump arrived in Washington, those old relationships were already part of the architecture of his power.

📌 What is RSI? The overbought/oversold indicator explained 

🔖 The relative strength index is one of the most widely used momentum oscillators in crypto trading, but most traders misread what it actually measures. This guide breaks down the RSI formula, explains how overbought and oversold signals work in practice, and covers the mistakes that turn a useful indicator into a losing strategy. Most traders learn RSI backwards. They start with the idea that 70 means “sell” and 30 means “buy,” treating the indicator like a traffic light for entries and exits. That mental model sounds logical, but it ignores what RSI actually calculates. The relative strength index does not measure whether an asset is expensive or cheap.

🌐 It measures how aggressively price has been moving in one direction compared to the other. Understanding that distinction is the difference between using RSI as a crutch and using it as a genuine analytical tool. RSI quantifies momentum by comparing the average size of recent up moves to the average size of recent down moves over a defined lookback period. The default period is 14, meaning the calculation considers the last 14 candles on whatever timeframe you are viewing.

📊 Average gain is the sum of all positive price changes over the lookback period divided by N. Average loss is the sum of all negative price changes (expressed as positive numbers) divided by N. Periods with no change count as zero for both. What this produces is a bounded oscillator. When gains completely dominate losses, RS becomes very large and RSI approaches 100. When losses dominate, RS approaches zero and RSI drops toward 0. A perfect balance between gains and losses produces an RS of 1 and an RSI of 50.
